FAQ

On this page

FAQ ​

How is a Run different from a chat session? ​

A chat session is one context that degrades as it compacts. A Run is durable: it has its own thread, its own frozen plan, a participant record per agent with a resumable session, one branch per coding participant, an append-only verification log, and a per-call usage ledger. It survives a server restart. See Runs.

Why did my task fail verification when the agent said it was done? ​

Because "done" is not the agent's call. A task reaches done only on a passed (or explicitly skipped) TaskVerification from something other than the agent that did the work — a shell command judged by exit code, or an independent verifier pass. Read verification.reason and failureKind; the latter tells you whether it was work_missing, semantic_failure, proof_missing, environment_failure, or provider_failure. See Plans & Tasks.

My check passes but the task is still not certified. Why? ​

Only a trusted check can mark a criterion proven, and a check is trusted only if it came from a source the run did not author — project config or an operator. The plan author writes both the criteria and the checks, so a self-authored {cmd: "true"} would otherwise certify anything. An untrusted check can still fail a task; it just cannot pass one.

Should I use guided or autonomous mode? ​

Guided for anything repeatable: the engine owns the dispatch loop, selects ready tasks from the frozen plan, and only advances on a passed verdict. Autonomous for genuinely exploratory work where re-planning mid-flight is the point. If you find yourself amending a guided plan repeatedly, the brief was the problem, not the mode.

Why does planVersion matter? ​

1 means the plan was set once and never amended — what a repeatable run should look like. Anything higher is drift, and originalChecklist lets you see exactly what changed. Without that pair, an amended plan is indistinguishable from a plan that was right the first time.

Where does memory live, and is it committed to my repo? ​

Memory lives in Saidi under memory/, as plain markdown. It is never committed to a client repo. Personal memory follows the human (memory/members/<userId>/global.md); project and agent memory is shared org-scoped workspace knowledge. Config lives in repos; memory lives here. See Memory & Conventions.

Why is my project agent asking permission for every change? ​

That is approval: confirm, the default. Change it in the project's memory-file frontmatter, or grant specific low-risk actions via auto-approve in Settings rather than switching the whole project to auto. See Project Policy.

Can Saidi merge or force-push? ​

No. Under the default branch: new policy, work lands on a saidi/* branch and a PR is opened. The merge is yours.

My reflex didn't fire. ​

Check in this order: (1) did the event reach the bus at all — the recent-event feed shows everything with a matched count; (2) did it match — matched: 0 means your source/type or match tree is wrong, and an invalid regex in matches fails closed; (3) was it skipped — the fire log records cooldown, dedup key, or maxFires; (4) is it pending on requireApproval; (5) does the reflex have a lastError. See Building a Reflex.

What is the changed operator comparing against? ​

The last value that specific reflex saw for that specific field. It keeps a small per-reflex-per-field memory — the only stateful operator. A first sighting counts as changed.

Why does a cost read as zero? ​

Two different reasons, and Saidi distinguishes them. unpriced on a usage entry means tokens were spent but the provider never reported a price (an aborted Anthropic call, or a custom endpoint with no rates configured). unreported means the call ran and not one request reported a token — those zeros are the absence of a measurement, not a measurement of zero. Neither is silently rendered as free.

What does costShared mean on a message? ​

The provider bills a turn once and reports no per-message cost, so a multi-turn message can only be apportioned. The shares sum to exactly what the turn cost, but no single one was quoted by the provider — so the UI says so rather than presenting an estimate as an invoice.

Two runs are touching the same repo. Is that safe? ​

Yes — a repo lock serialises delegations against one checkout, and custom agents take an equivalent agent lock. Custom agents also get a per-run workDir, so concurrent runs never share a directory.

What happens if the server crashes mid-delegation? ​

Every executing delegation is written to inFlights before it starts and cleared when it settles, so recovery can tell you exactly what was killed — its kind, target, task, and start time. Work you had already approved is marked so PRIME can re-delegate with approved: true instead of re-asking.

Does a single-user install need the org/tenant machinery? ​

It is already using it — single-owner is the degenerate case, with one org and one member. That is deliberate: a one-person workspace and a fifty-person one run the same code path rather than forking into two products. See Orgs, Auth & Permissions.

An MCP server shows as unavailable. ​

Most likely it needs an interactive OAuth authorisation that has never been completed. A headless or scheduled run cannot run that flow. Authorise it from an interactive session first, then re-probe. See Installing from the Marketplace.
